Non-Agricultural Labor Income - Constant 1973 dollars were used and the assumption was made that income per employee is constant regardless of race. The income results closely parallel the employment results; in addition, the greater relative involvement of Crows in the high-wage construction and mining sectors indicates substantial income consequences due to assumed levels of Crow involvement in coal development.
Figure III-3 shows total non-agricultural labor income estimates for both the Crow and non-Crow residents of the study area under the converging participating rate assumption (LFPR-2). The baseline income under both projected levels of coal development is shown, as is the income impact resulting from Westmoreland's most probable level of production (Scenario 1) under each projected level of coal development. Westmoreland's production level for this scenario would eventually increase Crow labor income by about $5 million over the baseline level. Income would reach approximately $12 million in the year 2000, about twice its 1975 level of $6 million.
When simultaneous development of other Crow coal leases is projected (AF-2), the increase in labor income is even more dramatic. The baseline study shows that the level of Crow labor income would be over $15 million by the early 1980's and close to $20 million by the end of the 1990's. As was the case with projected employment, Westmoreland Resources' most probable level of development does not make any significant difference on Crow labor income until the mid-1980's. After that time it adds about $5 million to the baseline, bringing the total to about $25 million, or nearly four times the 1975 level.
